Naively serving even a handful of concurrent users saturates GPU memory and leaves compute units idle. The entire field of LLM inference optimization exists to close the gap between the theoretical throughput of the hardware and the practical throughput of a serving system.

## 2. KV Caches: The Foundation

### 2.1 Why Caching Exists

In a transformer decoder, each layer computes attention as:

Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKᵀ / √d) · V

During generation, the query Q is a single new token, but K and V span the entire context. Recomputing K and V for all prior tokens at every step is O(n²) work repeated n times—quadratic waste. The KV cache stores the K and V tensors produced during the prefill (prompt-processing) phase so that each decode step only needs to compute K and V for the single new token and concatenate them to the cached history.

### 2.2 Memory Cost

For a model with L layers, H attention heads, head dimension d, and context length n, the KV cache per sequence is:

2 × L × H × d × n × bytes_per_element

For Llama-2-70B (80 layers, 8 KV heads with grouped-query attention, d=128, FP16), a 4096-token context consumes roughly 2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 4096 × 2 ≈ 1.3 GB per sequence. On an 80 GB A100, that limits you to ~60 concurrent sequences before weights are evicted.

This eliminates fragmentation, allows blocks to be shared across sequences (enabling prefix reuse), and lets the scheduler pack sequences densely.
